explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - This is an open-source, cross-platform management agent ("GLPI Agent") written primarily in Perl (with a small Go subcommand).  
   - Its purpose is to run on endpoints (Windows, Linux, macOS, Unix variants, ESX hosts), perform inventory/discovery/deployment tasks, and communicate results back to a GLPI server or act standalone via a local web interface (“Toolbox”).

2. High-level architecture and file-structure cues  
   - Top-level “bin/” holds CLI entry points (glpi-agent, glpi-inventory, glpi-netdiscovery, glpi-injector, etc.).  
   - “lib/GLPI/Agent” contains the agent core, scheduler, configuration loader, task runners, protocol handlers (HTTP client/server, SNMP, SOAP).  
   - “etc/” holds default configuration files.  
   - “share/html” provides HTML templates and static assets for the embedded web UI (Toolbox).  
   - “contrib/”, “debian/”, “snap/”, “contrib/windows/” house packaging and installer scripts.  
   - “t/” contains extensive unit and integration tests.  
   - “src/cmd” holds a Go-based injector tool.  
   - CI workflows are defined under “.github/workflows/”.

3. Core components to depict in your system design diagram  
   a. Agent Core  
      - Configuration Loader (reads etc/*.cfg)  
      - Scheduler/Plan Engine (determines when tasks run)  
      - Plugin/Task Manager (dynamically loads Task modules under lib/GLPI/Agent/Task)  
   b. Task Modules (group into logical tiers)  
      - Inventory Tasks (OS/hardware profiling across AIX, BSD, Linux, Windows, macOS, Solaris, Virtualization, ESX)  
      - Network Discovery Tasks  
      - Network Inventory Tasks  
      - Deploy Task (file copy, scripts, P2P)  
      - WakeOnLan Task  
      - Remote Inventory Task (SSH, WinRM)  
   c. Communication & Protocol Layers  
      - HTTP Client (GLPI protocol, FusionInventory, OCS)  
      - HTTP Server (optional web UI, plugins: BasicAuth, Inventory, Toolbox API)  
      - SNMP Client  
      - SOAP Client (VMware WS-Man)  
   d. External Tools & Programs  
      - dmidecode, lspci, hdparm, arp, ip, powercfg, SNMP utilities, etc.  
   e. CLI Interfaces  
      - bin/glpi-agent (main daemon/foreground runner)  
      - Other bin/ scripts invoking specific tasks or installers  
      - glpi-injector (Go tool)  
   f. Packaging & Deployment Pipelines  
      - snapcraft.yaml (Snap)  
      - debian/* (deb packages, postinst scripts)  
      - contrib/windows MSI toolchain  
      - MacOSX packaging scripts (munkipkg, hdiutil)  
      - GitHub Actions workflows (.github/workflows/*.yml)  
   g. Testing & CI  
      - t/ (Perl test suites)  
      - .github Actions badges and pipelines  

4. Relationships & data flows  
   - The Agent Core reads config → schedules Tasks → invokes Task modules → each Task may call External Tools or use internal Perl library to collect data → collected data flows into Protocol layer → HTTP Client sends to the GLPI Server (or FusionInventory endpoint) over HTTP/HTTPS.  
   - Optionally, the Agent exposes an HTTP Server for local web UI (Toolbox), so arrows flow: Agent Core ↔ HTTP Server ↔ Browser.  
   - SNMP and SOAP modules interact directly with network devices or ESX hosts.  
   - CLI scripts wrap Agent Core or specific Task calls for ad-hoc operations.  
   - Packaging pipelines consume the codebase and produce platform installers.

5. Architectural patterns & principles  
   - Modular/Plugin architecture: Task types are organized under namespace lib/GLPI/Agent/Task, auto-loaded via UNIVERSAL::require.  
   - Separation of concerns: distinct layers for configuration, scheduling, task execution, communication, and UI.  
   - Strategy pattern: each Task implements well-defined interfaces for collect/deploy/discovery.  
   - Extensibility: new Task modules or protocol handlers can be added without touching core scheduler.

6. Tailoring instructions for this open-source tool  
   - Emphasize the Agent’s pluggable Task framework and how new modules fit under lib/GLPI/Agent/Task.  
   - Show integration points with external programs (dmidecode, ssh, SNMP) via clear “External Tools” boundary.  
   - Highlight the Protocol layer's dual role (HTTP Client to GLPI Server, HTTP Server for local UI).  
   - Depict Packaging & CI as separate “DevOps” components feeding installers and artifact repositories.

7. Diagramming guidelines  
   - Use boxes for each major component (Core, Tasks, Protocols, External Tools, CLI, Packaging, CI).  
   - Label each box with directory paths (e.g., lib/GLPI/Agent/Task/Inventory) to tie back to file structure.  
   - Draw directional arrows:  
      • Core → Task Modules (invoke)  
      • Task Modules → External Tools (shell calls)  
      • Task Modules → Protocol Layer → GLPI Server (HTTP POST/GET)  
      • Browser → HTTP Server → Core (UI)  
   - Color-code by component type:  
      • Blue for Core & Scheduler  
      • Green for Task categories  
      • Orange for Protocol modules  
      • Gray for External Tools  
      • Purple for CLI & packaging  
   - Use different shapes:  
      • Rectangles for software modules  
      • Cylinders for external data stores or the remote GLPI server  
      • Parallelograms for CLI tools  

8. Detail level  
   - Be explicit: include all Task categories, external dependencies, packaging targets, and CI pipelines.  
   - Capture configuration inputs (etc/*.cfg) and resource directories (resources/) feeding Tasks.  
   - Ensure each arrow is annotated with the type of interaction (e.g., “invoke dmidecode”, “HTTP POST inventory data”).  

By following these steps, you’ll produce a comprehensive, accurate system-design diagram that reflects the true structure and extensibility of the GLPI Agent project.  
</explanation>
